title: Longest substring
description: Sliding window with a Set: expand the right edge, shrink the left while a duplicate sits in the window. O(n) time.

conversation.intro: How an interview about this problem would actually play out. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down the inputs.
sections.say:
"Let me make sure I have this right: longest substring of `s` with no repeating characters — by substring you mean contiguous, right? (As opposed to subsequence.)"

Then a few quick clarifying questions:
• Character set — ASCII only, or full Unicode?
• Empty string — return 0?
• Case sensitivity — is "aA" length 2 or 1?
• Return value — just the length, or the substring itself?
sections.why: Takes 20 seconds and signals that you don't dive into code blind. The character-set question matters: it sets the space bound. The contiguous-vs-subsequence question matters even more: if you misread it as subsequence, you'd build a completely different (and harder) solution.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(n²) solution before you discard it.
sections.say: "The brute force is: for every starting index `i`, walk forward with `j` and track seen characters in a Set. The moment you hit a repeat, record `j - i` and move `i` forward. That's O(n²) time, O(n) space — let me see if we can do better."
sections.why: Two reasons to name it out loud. (1) It proves you understand the problem before optimizing — interviewers worry about candidates who pattern-match straight to the clever answer. (2) It plants the seed for the real solution: the brute force is restarting the Set on every `i`. The optimization is literally just "don't restart — slide."

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern
sections.prompt: What signal in the problem points to sliding window?
sections.say: "'Longest contiguous X with property Y' is the canonical sliding-window trigger. And here the property — no repeats — is monotone under shrinkage: if `[l..r]` has a duplicate, removing chars from the left can only fix it, never break it. So once I move `r` forward, I never have to back up. One pass with `r`, a Set tracking what's in the window, and `l` only advances when forced."
sections.why: Naming the pattern *and* the property that makes the pattern apply is the move. "Sliding window" alone is a guess; "sliding window because the property is monotone in shrinkage" is a derivation. Interviewers grade on the second.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace through a couple of cases to make sure my model is right." Three inputs cover the interesting behaviors — a normal mix, an all-same-char degenerate case, and the L3 prompt's own input as a final sanity check.

examples.trace:
r=0 'a' → seen={a},     window [0,0], best=1
r=1 'b' → seen={a,b},   window [0,1], best=2
r=2 'c' → seen={a,b,c}, window [0,2], best=3
r=3 'a' → dup! delete s[0]='a', l=1. seen={b,c}. add 'a'. window [1,3], best=3
r=4 'b' → dup! delete s[1]='b', l=2. seen={c,a}. add 'b'. window [2,4], best=3
r=5 'c' → dup! delete s[2]='c', l=3. seen={a,b}. add 'c'. window [3,5], best=3
r=6 'b' → dup! delete s[3]='a', l=4. still dup. delete s[4]='b', l=5. add 'b'. window [5,6], best=3
r=7 'b' → dup! delete s[5]='c', l=6. still dup. delete s[6]='b', l=7. add 'b'. window [7,7], best=3

examples.note: Degenerate all-same-char — every step triggers a full shrink, but still O(n) amortized.
examples.trace:
r=0 'b' → seen={b}, window [0,0], best=1
r=1 'b' → dup! delete s[0]='b', l=1. add 'b'. window [1,1], best=1
r=2 'b' → dup! delete s[1]='b', l=2. add 'b'. window [2,2], best=1
r=3 'b' → dup! delete s[2]='b', l=3. add 'b'. window [3,3], best=1
r=4 'b' → dup! delete s[3]='b', l=4. add 'b'. window [4,4], best=1

examples.note: Sanity-check the L3 prompt's own input — the longest unique substring is "wke", not the prefix.
examples.trace:
r=0 'p' → seen={p},     window [0,0], best=1
r=1 'w' → seen={p,w},   window [0,1], best=2
r=2 'w' → dup! delete s[0]='p', l=1. still dup. delete s[1]='w', l=2. add 'w'. window [2,2], best=2
r=3 'k' → seen={w,k},   window [2,3], best=2
r=4 'e' → seen={w,k,e}, window [2,4], best=3
r=5 'w' → dup! delete s[2]='w', l=3. add 'w'. window [3,5], best=3

sections.why: Tracing surfaces the subtle bug — you have to delete `s[l]` *before* you increment `l`, otherwise you delete the wrong character. The all-same-char case also defends the O(n) claim: even when every step shrinks, each character still enters and exits the set exactly once. Catching both on the whiteboard is much less painful than catching them after the interviewer points out failing tests.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases to mention
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Before I declare it done, let me think about edges:
• Empty string → loop doesn't execute, best=0. ✓
• Single char → no duplicate, best=1. ✓
• All same char ("aaaa") → each new `r` triggers a full shrink, but every char still enters and exits the set exactly once, so still O(n). best=1.
• All unique ("abcdef") → `l` never moves, best=n.
• Unicode/emoji — `s[r]` indexes UTF-16 code units, not codepoints, so a single emoji could read as two halves. Worth flagging; the fix is `[...s]` to iterate by codepoint."
sections.why: Edge-case enumeration is the difference between "works on the example" and "production-ready". The Unicode call-out in particular shows depth — most candidates never think about it, and the interviewer either nods (impressed) or says "good catch but assume ASCII for now". Either outcome is good.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n) — even with the nested `while`, each character enters `seen` at most once and is removed at most once, so total work across the outer loop is bounded by 2n.

Space is O(min(n, |alphabet|)) — the Set never holds more than the alphabet size, which is 128 for ASCII, much smaller in practice.

If you wanted to extend to 'at most K distinct chars,' I'd swap the Set for a count-Map and shrink while `map.size > K`. Same template, different shrink condition."
sections.why: The amortized-analysis argument ("each char enters/exits once") is the right defense against an interviewer who pushes back with "but you have a nested loop, isn't that O(n²)?". The extension to 'at most K distinct' is unprompted bonus material that demonstrates you see the template, not just this one problem — that's how the same pattern shows up in Minimum Window Substring, Longest Substring with At Most K Distinct, etc.

reference.approach: Variable sliding window + Set of the window's chars
notes: Window is the substring s[l..r] inclusive — its length is r - l + 1.
Shrink with a while loop so the template generalizes to count-based windows.
Delete s[l] BEFORE incrementing l — otherwise you delete the wrong char.
reference.crux: Grow a window with a Set of its chars; when the new right char duplicates one inside, shrink from the left until it's gone — l never moves backward, so it's one pass.
cruxDistractors: For every start index, walk forward with a fresh Set until you hit a repeat, then move the start.
On a duplicate, jump l straight to the duplicate's position so it leaves the window in one step.
Count each character's frequency in a Map, then the answer is the count of chars that appear exactly once.

alternates.label: Index map (jump l directly)
alternates.when: Reach for this when you want l to jump straight past the duplicate in one step instead of shrinking one character at a time. Slightly harder to reason about (the max guard is easy to forget), but avoids the inner while loop and is often the variant interviewers expect if they say 'can you do it without a nested loop?'
notes: Map stores index, not a boolean — that's what enables the O(1) jump.
max(l, lastSeen.get(c) + 1) is load-bearing: without it, a stale entry (char last seen before l) would pull l backward and re-admit characters already outside the window.
Same O(n) / O(min(n,|alphabet|)) as the Set version; the constant factor differs but the class is identical.

questions.q: Window length expression for indices l..r inclusive?
questions.explain: Both ends are inside the window, so it spans `r - l + 1` characters. `r - l` counts the gaps between them, which undercounts by one — at `l === r` it would report 0 for a window holding one char.

questions.q: Why a Set rather than a count Map?
options: Set.has is O(1) while Map.get is O(log n) due to internal tree storage
We only need membership (in the window) — uniqueness is implicit
Maps can't be iterated in O(1), and the algorithm iterates the window each step
Sets handle the shrink step automatically — deleting from a Map would require checking count first
questions.explain: The window is never allowed a second copy of a char, so a count could only ever be 0 or 1 — `has` and `delete` carry all the information. Min Window Substring is where counts start mattering, because there `t` can demand two A's.

options: O(n) — each char enters and leaves the window once
questions.explain: The inner `while` looks like a nested loop, but `l` never moves backward — across the whole run the two pointers make at most 2n moves combined, so the shrink work is amortized rather than multiplied.

questions.q: When the right pointer sees a duplicate, you should:
options: Shrink from the left until the duplicate is removed
questions.explain: The earlier copy of `s[r]` can sit anywhere inside the window, so you `delete s[l]` and advance until it's gone. Jumping `l` straight to `r` throws away still-valid chars in between — on `"abac"` that loses the `b` and returns 2 instead of 3.

questions.q: In the Set-based version, why shrink with a `while` loop (deleting s[l] and l++) rather than a single l++?
options: You must keep deleting from the left until the duplicate of s[r] is actually gone from the window, which can take more than one step
The while loop sorts the characters
A single l++ would use more memory
questions.explain: The duplicate of s[r] can sit several positions inside the window, so you must delete and advance l repeatedly until it's removed before adding s[r].

questions.q: The index-map variant stores each char's LAST seen index. On a duplicate it jumps `l = max(l, lastSeen[c] + 1)`. Why the `max` with the current l?
options: A stale last-seen index could be left of l (already outside the window); max prevents l from moving backward
Because Math.max is required for indices
questions.explain: If the duplicate's last-seen index is behind the current l, moving l there would re-expand the window and re-admit chars already removed — max(l, ...) keeps l monotonically forward.

questions.q: What is the space complexity of the window?
options: O(min(n, |charset|)) — bounded by the alphabet size or the string length
questions.explain: The Set/map can hold at most one entry per distinct character, so it's capped by the alphabet (e.g. 128 for ASCII) or by n, whichever is smaller.

questions.q: Why is the overall time O(n) even though there's an inner while loop?
options: The while loop runs at most a constant number of times per outer step
Each character is added to the window once and removed once, so total left+right pointer moves are bounded by 2n
The while loop never actually executes
questions.explain: l only ever advances (never resets backward) and r advances once per step, so across the whole run each pointer moves at most n times — amortized O(n), not O(n^2).

exercises.prompt: Fill in the sliding-window with a Set.

L3.prompt: Write `lengthOfLongestSubstring(s)` returning the length of the longest substring without repeating chars. Log `lengthOfLongestSubstring("pwwkew")`.
hints: Slide a window [l, r] across the string.
While the new char is already in the Set, delete s[l] and l++.
Track best = r - l + 1 after each step.
